Revolut serves a self-hosted Chinese model to about 2,000 engineers and keeps Claude Code and Codex for the exceptions.

About 2,000 engineers at Revolut now write code by default with GLM, an open-weight model from the Chinese lab Z.ai that the digital bank hosts itself. Anthropic’s Claude Code and OpenAI’s Codex remain available, but only for exceptions. David Abitbol, who leads AI operations at Revolut, described the switch on October 13, 2026, at the AI Engineer conference in New York. He said the bill is now a tenth of what the company used to spend with Anthropic and OpenAI.

The talk and its full transcript are posted on the organizers’ website. Trending Topics, a European tech news site, and the startup data platform Dealroom covered it on the morning of November 3. The Register followed that evening with a headline about AI coding costs cut tenfold.

Abitbol walked through three stages, measured on a sample of about 2,000 engineers. Revolut tracks two metrics: coding time, in hours, and lead time, in days, from the moment an engineer picks up a feature to the moment it is merged and ready to deploy.

In early 2025, the company rolled out Gemini. Coding time fell 20% and lead time 10%, according to the chart he showed. Claude Code came next, launched at scale in early 2026 with strict budget caps. At the time, its impact was small.

“We were highly skeptical about the cost of AI,” Abitbol said. “We were seeing engineers spend $1,000 a month, $10,000 a month with not so much ROI.”

In April 2026, Revolut started hosting GLM 5.1 itself. From there, the chart shows a 60% improvement in coding time and a 70% improvement in lead time.

Abitbol’s conclusion is that coding is not necessarily the bottleneck in engineering. Engineers get a lot of time back when they no longer have to dig through their inboxes or wrestle with Jira and Confluence. With unlimited tokens, they stop saving them “for the end of the quarter or the most difficult task.”

Revolut runs GLM 5.3, the current version, on 56 Nvidia B200 GPUs for about 2,000 engineers. In GPU count, that is equivalent to seven eight-GPU DGX B200 systems, The Register notes. The blended cost works out to about 30 cents per million tokens. “The billing is flat, we don’t have any bill shock at the end of the month, and the frontier is the exception,” Abitbol said.

He sets two targets. The first token has to arrive in under three seconds; past five, his Slack inbox “starts to blow up.” Generation speed matters less. In his view, 200 tokens per second is enough, because engineers run tasks in parallel and check back when they’re done instead of watching the model think in real time.

Hitting the three-second target took tuning. According to the slide described on the organizers’ page, time to first token dropped from 14.26 seconds during the migration to 1.68 seconds in the stable setup, on the same number of GPUs, while requests per second rose 76%. Abitbol pointed to FP4 quantization on Blackwell chips and to splitting the model across eight GPUs instead of four, which leaves enough memory for the KV cache. He also advised tracking the cache hit rate, which matters a lot for coding, where the same context keeps coming back.

Long context, in his words, is “a scam”: even if you can serve a million tokens, 256,000 is what this work needs. A guide to running AI locally in a business explains what drives time to first token and how much memory an open model needs.

GLM handles text only, so a router sends requests that include images to other models, such as Gemini or GPT Luna. The internal endpoints follow OpenAI’s API format, which lets engineers keep the coding tools they prefer, including OpenCode and Codex.

Abitbol acknowledged the “stigma” around Chinese models. His answer turns on where the data goes: Revolut downloads the published weights and runs them on infrastructure of its choosing, without going through an inference service based in China. He said the GPUs can sit in the United States, the European Union, the United Kingdom or Israel, with providers that keep no data by default.

Revolut is regulated as a bank in the EU and keeps a human in the loop on all coding tasks, so it doesn’t have to present them to its regulator as autonomous agents.

Each agent runs in a sandbox whose rules set what it can execute without approval: “you can allow grep but not gradle” (grep searches text in files; Gradle is a build tool). The same setup is meant to guard against insider misuse and prompt injection. Detailed logs make it possible to reconstruct an incident.

GLM 5.1 was released under the MIT license. GLM 5.3, released in late August, uses Z.ai’s own license. Commercial use is free, but a company that sells API access to models and brings in more than $10 billion in revenue over 12 months must first pas

items.title: Revolut sidelines Claude Code for a self-hosted Chinese model, says it pays 90% less
